subtopics.title: The Data Cycle and the Question Worth Asking

questions.question: Which of these is the correct order of the data cycle?
options: Pose a question, collect, organise and classify, summarise and represent, analyse, report
Collect, pose a question, summarise, organise, report
Summarise, collect, pose a question, report, organise
Organise, collect, analyse, pose a question, report

questions.question: A commuter's queueing time of 23,5 minutes is an example of which type of data?
options: Categorical data
Continuous numerical data
Discrete numerical data
Secondary categorical data

questions.question: The class uses the association's departure log book instead of timing commuters themselves. This makes the data:
options: primary data, because the class is using them for its own question
biased data, because log books are never accurate
categorical data, because a log book contains names
secondary data, because they were recorded by someone else for another purpose

questions.question: Which choice would have introduced the most serious bias into the rank study?
options: Timing commuters to the nearest minute
Timing fifteen commuters spread across the morning
Timing only the five o'clock rush, or only commuters who came to complain
Using a stopwatch rather than asking commuters to estimate

subtopics.title: Tallies, Frequency Tables and Class Intervals

questions.question: In the class's frequency table, the interval 20 to 39 minutes has a frequency of:
Why are intervals of "0 to 20" and "20 to 40" unacceptable?
options: Because the intervals are too narrow
Because intervals must always start at 1
Because they overlap, so a wait of exactly 20 minutes belongs in two rows
Because continuous data may never be grouped

questions.question: What check should be done on every frequency table before it is used?
options: That the frequencies add up to the number of values collected
That every interval holds at least one value
That the biggest frequency sits in the first row
That the intervals run from largest to smallest

questions.question: What is lost when continuous data are grouped into class intervals?
options: The unit of measurement
The total number of values
Nothing — the table keeps all the original information
The individual values themselves, so exact figures such as three waits of 30 minutes can no longer be read off

questions.question: The fifteen queueing times total 540 minutes. What is the mean?
options: 30 minutes
45 minutes
36 minutes
54 minutes

questions.question: For the fifteen ordered values, which position holds the median, and what is it?
options: Position 8; median 30 minutes
Position 7,5; median 29 minutes
Position 8; median 36 minutes
Position 15; median 96 minutes

questions.question: The range of the queueing times is:
options: 96 minutes
90 minutes
36 minutes
30 minutes

questions.question: Which measure of centre can be used for categorical data such as the destination of a trip?
options: The mean
The median
The range
The mode

questions.question: Why is the mean of 36 minutes higher than the median of 30 minutes?
options: Because the mode is also 30
Because three commuters waited 60, 72 and 96 minutes, and those outliers pull the mean upward
Because the median was taken from unordered data
Because 15 is an odd number of values

questions.question: The association wants the total commuter time the queue swallowed. Which summary rebuilds that total?
options: The median, because it is the typical wait
The mode, because it is the most common wait
The mean, because mean × number of commuters gives back 540 minutes
The range, because it spans all the values

questions.question: What is the stated weakness of the range?
options: It is built from only two values, so a single unusual case can distort it
It cannot be calculated for continuous data
It always equals the mean minus the median
It ignores the smallest value in the data set

questions.question: Which conclusion best matches the rank's data?
options: Every commuter waits about an hour, so more taxis are needed all day
The rank is quick, since the mode is only 30 minutes
The typical wait is 30 minutes; the real problem is a long tail of very long waits
Nothing can be concluded, because the mean and median disagree

subtopics.title: Asking a Question the Numbers Can Answer

questions.question: Why is "Do we spend too much on transport?" a poor question to investigate?
options: Because transport spending is categorical data
Because it asks about a household rather than a school
Because it needs a tally table
Because "too much" cannot be measured, so no number could settle it

questions.question: Which of these can NOT be added together?
options: Rands spent on taxis by each person
The bus companies people ride with, such as MyCiTi and Golden Arrow
Minutes queued by each commuter
Taxis counted on the rank each hour

questions.question: "Don't you agree the queue is a disaster?" is a poor survey question because it:
options: produces continuous data instead of discrete data
cannot be tallied
leans towards the answer it wants, instead of asking neutrally
requires secondary data

questions.question: What is the first thing to do with a jumbled list of values?
options: Put them in order from smallest to largest
Calculate the average
Draw a graph
Round them all to the nearest ten

questions.question: In a tally, why is every fifth stroke drawn across the four before it?
options: To mark the end of a class interval
So the marks count themselves in fives and are easy to total
To show that value is the mode
To flag an outlier

questions.question: The five piles of queue times contain 4, 6, 2, 2 and 1 commuters. What does adding them confirm?
options: That the mode is in the second pile
That the intervals do not overlap
That all 15 commuters have been counted once, with none lost or double-counted
That the range is 90 minutes

subtopics.title: The Middle, the Most, the Average and the Stretch

questions.question: The Simplifier calls the mean the "sharing-out number". For the rank data that number is:
options: 30 minutes
36 minutes
540 minutes
90 minutes

questions.question: If there had been an EVEN number of commuters, how would the middle value be found?
options: Take the two middle values and split the difference between them
Take the larger of the two middle values
Use the mode instead
The median cannot be found for an even number of values

questions.question: Which everyday comparison does the Simplifier use for the mean being dragged upward?
options: A taxi that is always full
A tally counted twice
A washing basket that never empties
One cousin with a big contract phone hauling up the family's "average airtime spend"

questions.question: What does the Simplifier say a complete answer must include, beyond the number itself?
options: The unit, and a plain sentence about what should actually be done
A second calculation using a different method
A graph of the data
The raw data listed in full
